code: #' Calculate Classification Entropy #' #' Computes the entropy of posterior class membership probabilities. #' Higher values indicate greater classification uncertainty. #' #' @param posterior_probs Numeric matrix of posterior probabilities #'   (rows = individuals, columns = classes) #' @param method Character string specifying entropy calculation method. #'   Options: "standard" (default), "relative", "normalized" #' #' @return Numeric value representing entropy. For "standard" method, #'   ranges from 0 (perfect classification) to log(K) where K is the #'   number of classes. #' #' @details #' The entropy measure quantifies classification uncertainty. Perfect #' classification (all posterior probabilities = 0 or 1) yields entropy = 0. #' Maximum uncertainty (equal probabilities across classes) yields entropy = log(K). #' #' @examples #' # Perfect classification (low entropy) #' probs1 <- matrix(c(1, 0, 0, 0, 1, 0), ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE) #' calculate_entropy(probs1)  # Returns 0 #' #' # Uncertain classification (high entropy) #' probs2 <- matrix(c(0.33, 0.33, 0.34), ncol = 3) #' calculate_entropy(probs2)  # Returns ~1.099 (close to log(3)) #' #' @export #' @seealso \code{\link{classification_quality}} for related diagnostics

text: Follow tidyverse style guide: Naming conventions: - Functions: snake_case (e.g., calculate_entropy, gmm_survey) - Variables: snake_case (e.g., posterior_probs, n_classes) - Classes: PascalCase (e.g., SurveyMixr, InfluenceDiagnostics) - Constants: UPPER_SNAKE_CASE (rare R) Code organization: - Keep functions focused (single responsibility principle) - Use meaningful variable names (avoid x, tmp, data1) - Comment complex algorithms non-obvious code - Limit line length 80 characters - Use spaces around operators (x + y, x+y) - Indent 2 spaces (tabs) Good example: Bad example (avoid):
code: calculate_entropy <- function(posterior_probs, method = "standard") {   # Validate input   if (!is.matrix(posterior_probs)) {     stop("posterior_probs must be a matrix")   }    # Calculate standard entropy   # Avoid log(0) by adding small constant   log_probs <- log(posterior_probs + 1e-10)   entropy <- -sum(posterior_probs * log_probs, na.rm = TRUE)    # Apply method-specific adjustments   if (method == "normalized") {     n_classes <- ncol(posterior_probs)     max_entropy <- log(n_classes)     entropy <- entropy / max_entropy   }    return(entropy) } calc_e <- function(pp, m = "s") {   lp <- log(pp + 1e-10)   e <- -sum(pp * lp, na.rm = T)   if (m == "n") e <- e / log(ncol(pp))   return(e) }

title: Categorical Outcomes in Growth Mixture Models
text: continuous outcomes (e.g., test scores, depression symptoms) common growth mixture modeling, many developmental behavioral outcomes categorical: Binary: Smoking (yes/), high school graduation (yes/), clinical diagnosis (yes/) Ordinal: Likert scales, severity ratings, frequency categories Count: Number delinquent acts, number hospitalizations, number romantic partners vignette demonstrates use surveymixr growth mixture models categorical outcomes properly accounting complex survey design features.

title: Categorical Outcomes in Growth Mixture Models
text: Traditional GMM assumes continuous, normally distributed outcomes. categorical data, assumption violated, leading : Biased parameter estimates - Treating ordered categories continuous can distort growth trajectories Incorrect standard errors - Violates assumptions residual distributions Invalid inferences - Statistical tests may anti-conservative Poor model fit - Continuous models don’t capture ceiling/floor effects categorical data surveymixr package addresses issues implementing appropriate link functions likelihood computations outcome type.

title: Categorical Outcomes in Growth Mixture Models
text: Let’s examine developmental trajectories smoking initiation (0 = never smoked, 1 = ever smoked) ages 12-18.
code: library(surveymixr)  # Simulate binary outcome data set.seed(123) smoking_data <- simulate_gmm_survey(   n_individuals = 2000,   n_times = 7,  # Ages 12-18   n_classes = 3,   time_scores = 12:18,   outcome_type = "binary",   class_proportions = c(0.60, 0.25, 0.15),  # Never, Late starters, Early starters   design = "stratified_cluster",   n_strata = 4,   n_clusters = 100,   seed = 123 )  # Rename for clarity names(smoking_data)[names(smoking_data) == "outcome"] <- "ever_smoked" names(smoking_data)[names(smoking_data) == "time"] <- "age"

title: Categorical Outcomes in Growth Mixture Models
code: # Fit 3-class model with probit link fit_smoking <- gmm_survey_binary(   data = smoking_data,   id = "id",   time = "age",   outcome = "ever_smoked",   n_classes = 3,   growth_model = "linear",   link = "probit",  # or "logit"   strata = "stratum",   cluster = "psu",   weights = "weight",   starts = 200,   cores = 4 )  # View results summary(fit_smoking)

title: Categorical Outcomes in Growth Mixture Models
text: binary outcomes probit link, growth parameters latent continuous scale (underlying propensity smoke):
code: # Extract parameters params <- coef(fit_smoking)  # For Class 1 (Never smokers): # Intercept at age 12: -2.5 (very low propensity) # Slope: 0.05 (minimal increase over time) # Probability of smoking at age 12: pnorm(-2.5) ≈ 0.006 (0.6%)  # For Class 3 (Early starters): # Intercept at age 12: 0.5 (moderate propensity) # Slope: 0.30 (rapid increase) # Probability at age 12: pnorm(0.5) ≈ 0.69 (69%) # Probability at age 18: pnorm(0.5 + 0.30*6) ≈ pnorm(2.3) ≈ 0.99 (99%)

title: Categorical Outcomes in Growth Mixture Models
code: # Plot on probability scale plot(fit_smoking, scale = "probability")  # Plot on latent scale plot(fit_smoking, scale = "latent")  # Class proportions class_proportions(fit_smoking) #   Class 1 (Never): 62% #   Class 2 (Late starters): 24% #   Class 3 (Early starters): 14%

title: Categorical Outcomes in Growth Mixture Models
text: Probit advantages: - Direct connection normal distribution theory - Standard GMM literature (Mplus uses probit) - Easier theoretical justification Logit advantages: - Odds ratio interpretation - common applied research - Slightly heavier tails (robust outliers)
code: # Probit link (default) fit_probit <- gmm_survey_binary(   data = smoking_data,   id = "id", time = "age", outcome = "ever_smoked",   n_classes = 3, link = "probit", starts = 100 )  # Logit link (easier interpretation via odds ratios) fit_logit <- gmm_survey_binary(   data = smoking_data,   id = "id", time = "age", outcome = "ever_smoked",   n_classes = 3, link = "logit", starts = 100 )  # Compare fit compare_models(fit_probit, fit_logit) # Results typically very similar; choose based on interpretation preference

title: Categorical Outcomes in Growth Mixture Models
text: Ordinal outcomes natural ordering unequal spacing categories.
code: # Simulate ordinal outcome: self-rated health (1=Poor, 2=Fair, 3=Good, 4=Very Good, 5=Excellent) health_data <- simulate_gmm_survey(   n_individuals = 1500,   n_times = 6,   n_classes = 3,   outcome_type = "ordinal",   n_categories = 5,   design = "stratified_cluster",   seed = 456 )  names(health_data)[names(health_data) == "outcome"] <- "health_rating"

title: Categorical Outcomes in Growth Mixture Models
text: proportional odds (PO) model standard ordinal outcomes: P(Yit≤j|Class k)=Φ(τj−ηitk) P(Y_{} \leq j | \text{Class } k) = \Phi(\tau_j - \eta_{itk}) τ1<τ2<τ3<τ4\tau_1 < \tau_2 < \tau_3 < \tau_4 threshold parameters ηitk=β0k+β1kt\eta_{itk} = \beta_{0k} + \beta_{1k} t linear predictor.
code: # Fit 3-class ordinal model fit_health <- gmm_survey_ordinal(   data = health_data,   id = "id",   time = "time",   outcome = "health_rating",   n_classes = 3,   n_categories = 5,   ordinal_model = "proportional_odds",   strata = "stratum",   cluster = "psu",   weights = "weight",   starts = 200 )  summary(fit_health)

title: Categorical Outcomes in Growth Mixture Models
code: # Extract threshold parameters thresholds <- extract_thresholds(fit_health)  # For Class 1: # τ₁ = -1.5  (Poor vs Fair+) # τ₂ = 0.2   (Poor+Fair vs Good+) # τ₃ = 1.3   (Poor+Fair+Good vs Very Good+) # τ₄ = 2.1   (Poor+Fair+Good+Very Good vs Excellent)  # Probability of "Good" or better at time 0: # P(Y ≥ 3) = 1 - Φ(τ₂ - η) = 1 - Φ(0.2 - β₀)

title: Categorical Outcomes in Growth Mixture Models
code: # Test proportional odds assumption test_po_assumption(fit_health)  # If violated, consider: # 1. Adjacent category model fit_adjacent <- gmm_survey_ordinal(   data = health_data,   id = "id", time = "time", outcome = "health_rating",   n_classes = 3, n_categories = 5,   ordinal_model = "adjacent_category" )  # 2. Continuation ratio model (for sequential outcomes)

title: Categorical Outcomes in Growth Mixture Models
text: Count outcomes non-negative integers representing frequency events.
code: # Simulate count outcome: number of delinquent acts per year delinquency_data <- simulate_gmm_survey(   n_individuals = 2500,   n_times = 5,   n_classes = 3,   outcome_type = "count",   design = "cluster",   seed = 789 )  names(delinquency_data)[names(delinquency_data) == "outcome"] <- "num_acts"

title: Categorical Outcomes in Growth Mixture Models
text: Basic count model assumes Poisson distribution:
code: fit_poisson <- gmm_survey_count(   data = delinquency_data,   id = "id",   time = "time",   outcome = "num_acts",   n_classes = 3,   count_model = "poisson",   cluster = "psu",   weights = "weight",   starts = 200 )  # Interpretation on log scale: # log(λ) = β₀ + β₁ * time # λ is the expected count  # Convert to multiplicative effects: coef_poisson <- coef(fit_poisson) exp(coef_poisson)  # Incidence rate ratios

title: Categorical Outcomes in Growth Mixture Models
text: Real count data often exhibit overdispersion (variance > mean), violating Poisson assumption.
code: # Check for overdispersion check_overdispersion(fit_poisson) # Dispersion ratio: 3.2 (overdispersed!)  # Use negative binomial model fit_nb <- gmm_survey_count(   data = delinquency_data,   id = "id", time = "time", outcome = "num_acts",   n_classes = 3,   count_model = "negative_binomial",   starts = 200 )  # Compare fit compare_models(fit_poisson, fit_nb) # BIC favors negative binomial: 12450 vs 12890

title: Categorical Outcomes in Growth Mixture Models
text: data contain excess zeros (e.g., many adolescents commit zero delinquent acts):
code: # Check proportion of zeros mean(delinquency_data$num_acts == 0)  # 45% zeros  # Fit zero-inflated Poisson fit_zip <- gmm_survey_count(   data = delinquency_data,   id = "id", time = "time", outcome = "num_acts",   n_classes = 3,   count_model = "zero_inflated",   starts = 200 )  summary(fit_zip)  # Model has two parts: # 1. Zero-inflation: P(structural zero) # 2. Count process: Poisson(λ) for non-structural zeros

code: # Compare 1-5 class models selection_binary <- gmm_select(   data = smoking_data,   id = "id", time = "age", outcome = "ever_smoked",   classes = 1:5,   outcome_type = "binary",   criteria = c("AIC", "BIC", "aBIC"),   starts = 100 )  plot(selection_binary)  # For categorical outcomes, BLRT may be computationally intensive # Consider using LMR test instead: lmr_results <- lmr_sequential(selection_binary$models) print(lmr_results)

text: Categorical outcomes generally require larger samples continuous: Binary: N ≥ 500 per class stable estimation Ordinal (5 categories): N ≥ 300 per class Count: Depends mean; higher means need smaller N

code: # Increase random starts fit_stable <- gmm_survey_binary(   data = smoking_data,   id = "id", time = "age", outcome = "ever_smoked",   n_classes = 3,   starts = 500,  # More starts for stability   cores = 4 )  # Check convergence diagnose_convergence(fit_stable)  # If problems persist: # 1. Check for separation issues diagnose_separation(fit_stable)  # 2. Try different link functions # 3. Simplify growth model (linear instead of quadratic) # 4. Check for outliers in time variable

text: happens treat categorical data continuous?
code: # WRONG: Treat binary as continuous fit_wrong <- gmm_survey(   data = smoking_data,   id = "id", time = "age",   outcome = "ever_smoked",  # Binary treated as continuous!   n_classes = 3,   starts = 100 )  # CORRECT: Use binary model fit_correct <- gmm_survey_binary(   data = smoking_data,   id = "id", time = "age",   outcome = "ever_smoked",   n_classes = 3,   link = "probit",   starts = 100 )  # Compare: # - Class proportions differ # - Parameter estimates not comparable # - Standard errors underestimated in continuous model # - Fit indices favor categorical model

title: Enhanced Model Selection Methods
text: One challenging aspects growth mixture modeling determining optimal number latent classes. Unlike traditional clustering factor analysis, ’s single definitive test. Instead, researchers must triangulate evidence multiple sources: Statistical fit indices (BIC, AIC, aBIC) Likelihood ratio tests (BLRT, LMR) Classification quality (Entropy, AvePP) Cross-validation (--sample prediction) Theoretical meaningfulness Practical utility vignette demonstrates enhanced model selection tools surveymixr v0.2.0+, including: Lo-Mendell-Rubin (LMR) Test: Fast asymptotic alternative BLRT Cross-Validation: --sample prediction accuracy Integrated Comparison: Comprehensive model selection workflow

title: Enhanced Model Selection Methods
text: Growth mixture models present unique challenges:
code: # Unlike k-means clustering: # - No "true" number of classes (latent construct) # - Non-nested models (can't use standard LRT) # - Boundary conditions (variance can't be negative) # - Label switching (class order arbitrary) # - Local maxima (multiple solutions exist)  # Unlike factor analysis: # - No scree plot equivalent # - No eigen value > 1 rule # - No parallel analysis

title: Enhanced Model Selection Methods
text: Different criteria answer different questions:

title: Enhanced Model Selection Methods
text: easiest way compare models using gmm_select():
code: library(surveymixr) data(mcs_simulated)  # Compare 1-5 class models with multiple criteria selection <- gmm_select(   data = mcs_simulated,   id = "id",   time = "age",   outcome = "selfcontrol",   classes = 1:5,   strata = "stratum",   cluster = "cluster",   weights = "weight",   criteria = c("BIC", "entropy", "BLRT"),  # Multiple criteria   blrt_samples = 100,   starts = 200,   cores = 4 )  # View results print(selection) plot(selection)

title: Enhanced Model Selection Methods
text: Note: LMR tests automatically computed gmm_select(). Use standalone lmr_test() lmr_sequential() functions LMR-based model comparison (see examples ).

title: Enhanced Model Selection Methods
text: LMR test (Lo2001?) provides asymptotic approximation likelihood ratio test comparing kk vs. k−1k-1 classes, without requiring bootstrap resampling. Null hypothesis: k−1k-1 classes sufficient Alternative hypothesis: kk classes fit better Key advantage: 10-100x faster BLRT

title: Enhanced Model Selection Methods
text: Use LMR : ✅ Sample size large (N>500N > 500) ✅ need quick preliminary results ✅ BLRT computationally expensive ✅ ’re fitting many models exploration Use BLRT : ✅ Sample size small moderate ✅ Final decision-making (publication) ✅ Results borderline ✅ Computational resources available

title: Enhanced Model Selection Methods
text: Output:
code: # Fit individual models fit2 <- gmm_survey(   data = mcs_simulated,   id = "id", time = "age", outcome = "selfcontrol",   n_classes = 2, starts = 200 )  fit3 <- gmm_survey(   data = mcs_simulated,   id = "id", time = "age", outcome = "selfcontrol",   n_classes = 3, starts = 200 )  # LMR test: Is 3-class better than 2-class? lmr_result <- lmr_test(fit3, fit2, adjusted = TRUE) print(lmr_result) Lo-Mendell-Rubin Likelihood Ratio Test ======================================================  Model Comparison:   H0: 2-class model is sufficient   H1: 3-class model fits better  Log-Likelihoods:   2-class: -15234.56   3-class: -15198.23  Test Statistics:   LMR statistic: 72.66   Adjusted LMR:  68.92   Scaling factor: 1.054   Degrees of freedom: 5  P-values:   LMR:      <0.001   Adjusted: 0.002 (recommended)  Conclusion:   Reject H0: 3-class model fits significantly better than   2-class model (p = 0.002)

what: Bootstrap Confidence Intervals for Model Selection
title: Enhanced Model Selection Methods
code: # NOT for hypothesis testing, but for uncertainty quantification  # Bootstrap BIC differences bootstrap_selection <- function(data, B = 100) {   bic_diff <- numeric(B)    for (b in 1:B) {     # Resample individuals (not observations)     ids <- unique(data$id)     boot_ids <- sample(ids, replace = TRUE)     boot_data <- data[data$id %in% boot_ids, ]      # Fit models     fit3_boot <- gmm_survey(boot_data, ..., n_classes = 3, starts = 50)     fit4_boot <- gmm_survey(boot_data, ..., n_classes = 4, starts = 50)      # Store BIC difference     bic_diff[b] <- BIC(fit3_boot) - BIC(fit4_boot)   }    return(bic_diff) }  # Run bootstrap bic_boot <- bootstrap_selection(mcs_simulated, B = 100)  # 95% CI for BIC difference quantile(bic_boot, c(0.025, 0.975)) # If CI includes 0, evidence is weak

title: Enhanced Model Selection Methods
text: Key takeaways model selection surveymixr: Use multiple criteria - single test definitive LMR test - Fast preliminary screening (10-100x faster BLRT) Cross-validation - Gold standard prediction, computationally expensive Sequential approach - Screen LMR, validate CV Classification quality - Entropy > 0.80, smallest class > 5% Theoretical fit - Classes must make substantive sense Stability - Refit different starts, check convergence Recommended workflow:
code: 1. Quick screening (LMR + BIC, 100 starts)    ↓ 2. Focused refitting (500+ starts for promising models)    ↓ 3. Cross-validation (top 2-3 candidates)    ↓ 4. Detailed diagnostics (entropy, class sizes, convergence)    ↓ 5. Theoretical evaluation    ↓ 6. Final decision + sensitivity analysis

text: Growth mixture modeling can computationally intensive. guide provides strategies optimizing performance managing computational resources.

title: Performance Optimization for Growth Mixture Modeling
text: GMM estimation involves: E-step: Compute posterior class probabilities individuals (N × K operations) M-step: Update parameters using weighted least squares Multiple random starts: Repeat entire process 500-1000+ times Standard errors: Numerical derivatives bootstrap Time complexity: O(N × K × p × n_iter × n_starts) : - N = number individuals - K = number classes - p = number parameters - n_iter = iterations convergence - n_starts = random starts (500+)

title: Performance Optimization for Growth Mixture Modeling

title: Performance Optimization for Growth Mixture Modeling
code: # Benchmark function benchmark_gmm <- function(n_starts = 200, n_cores = 4) {   start_time <- Sys.time()    fit <- gmm_survey(     data = mcs_simulated,     id = "id",     time = "age",     outcome = "selfcontrol",     n_classes = 3,     growth_model = "linear",     starts = n_starts,     cores = n_cores,     store_data = FALSE   )    end_time <- Sys.time()   elapsed <- as.numeric(difftime(end_time, start_time, units = "secs"))    list(     time_seconds = elapsed,     time_minutes = elapsed / 60,     n_starts = n_starts,     n_cores = n_cores,     converged = fit@converged   ) }  # Test different configurations configs <- expand.grid(   starts = c(100, 200, 500),   cores = c(1, 2, 4) )  results <- plyr::ldply(1:nrow(configs), function(i) {   config <- configs[i, ]   benchmark_gmm(config$starts, config$cores) })  print(results)

title: Analyzing Distal Outcomes with R3STEP
text: identifying latent classes using growth mixture modeling, researchers often want examine classes differ distal outcomes - variables measured separate trajectory analysis. Examples distal outcomes: - Delinquency (self-control trajectories) - Academic achievement (engagement trajectories) - Health outcomes (stress trajectories) - Employment status (skill development trajectories) Problem: Simply assigning individuals likely class comparing means biased due classification error (Bakk et al. 2013). Solution: R3STEP method accounts classification uncertainty, providing unbiased estimates class differences distal outcomes.

what: Step 1: Fit Unconditional Growth Mixture Model
title: Analyzing Distal Outcomes with R3STEP
text: First, fit GMM without distal outcome. ensures class formation isn’t influenced distal variable.
code: # Load example data data(mcs_simulated)  # Fit 3-class model of self-control trajectories gmm_fit <- gmm_survey(   data = mcs_simulated,   id = "id",   time = "age",   outcome = "selfcontrol",   n_classes = 3,   growth_model = "linear",   strata = "stratum",   cluster = "cluster",   weights = "weight",   starts = 500,   cores = 4 )  summary(gmm_fit)  # Create person-level data for R3STEP analysis # R3STEP requires one row per individual person_data <- mcs_simulated[!duplicated(mcs_simulated$id), ]

code: # Get posterior probabilities (stored in fitted model) posterior_probs <- gmm_fit@posterior_probs  # Most likely class assignment most_likely_class <- apply(posterior_probs, 1, which.max)  table(most_likely_class)

code: # Analyze delinquency as distal outcome r3_result <- r3step(   gmm_object = gmm_fit,   distal_vars = "delinquency",   data = person_data,   method = "BCH"  # Recommended method )  summary(r3_result)

title: Analyzing Distal Outcomes with R3STEP
text: surveymixr implements three R3STEP methods:

title: Analyzing Distal Outcomes with R3STEP
text: Bolck-Croon-Hagenaars (Bolck et al. 2004) method uses weights correct classification error. Advantages: - Computationally efficient - Works well survey weights - Provides survey-adjusted standard errors - widely used use: Default choice applications
code: result_bch <- r3step(   gmm_object = gmm_fit,   distal_vars = "academic_achievement",   data = person_data,   method = "BCH" )  # View class-specific means result_bch@class_means  # View omnibus test (do classes differ overall?) result_bch@test_results$omnibus_test  # View pairwise comparisons result_bch@test_results$pairwise_tests

title: Analyzing Distal Outcomes with R3STEP
text: Maximum likelihood approach jointly models class membership distal outcome. Advantages: - Theoretically optimal - Handles complex relationships Disadvantages: - computationally intensive - May unstable small classes use: BCH assumptions violated publication comparisons
code: result_ml <- r3step(   gmm_object = gmm_fit,   distal_vars = "delinquency",   data = person_data,   method = "ML",   cores = 4  # Can parallelize )  summary(result_ml)

title: Analyzing Distal Outcomes with R3STEP
text: Research Question: self-control trajectory classes differ academic achievement? Results Interpretation:
code: # Step 1: Fit GMM (already done above)  # Step 2+3: Analyze achievement as distal achievement_result <- r3step(   gmm_object = gmm_fit,   distal_vars = "academic_achievement",   data = person_data,   method = "BCH" )  summary(achievement_result)  # Plot results plot(achievement_result)  # Export table for publication library(gt) gt_table <- gt(achievement_result@class_means) %>%   tab_header(title = "Academic Achievement by Self-Control Trajectory Class") %>%   fmt_number(columns = c(mean, se, lower_ci, upper_ci), decimals = 2)  gtsave(gt_table, "achievement_table.html") Class 1 (High self-control):    Mean = 105.2 (SE = 1.2) Class 2 (Moderate):              Mean = 95.3 (SE = 1.5) Class 3 (Low self-control):     Mean = 85.1 (SE = 1.8)  Omnibus test: F(2, 997) = 68.4, p < .001 All pairwise differences significant (p < .001)

title: Analyzing Distal Outcomes with R3STEP
text: Test multiple outcomes separately (multiple comparison correction):
code: # Analyze multiple outcomes outcomes <- c("delinquency", "academic_achievement", "ses")  results_list <- lapply(outcomes, function(outcome) {   r3step(     gmm_object = gmm_fit,     distal_vars = outcome,     data = person_data,     method = "BCH"   ) })  names(results_list) <- outcomes  # Apply Bonferroni correction n_tests <- length(outcomes) alpha_adjusted <- 0.05 / n_tests  # 0.05 / 3 = 0.0167  # Check which are significant after correction for (outcome in outcomes) {   p <- results_list[[outcome]]@test_results$omnibus_test$p_value   sig <- ifelse(p < alpha_adjusted, "Yes", "No")   cat(sprintf("%s: p = %.4f, Significant = %s\n", outcome, p, sig)) }

title: Analyzing Distal Outcomes with R3STEP
text: Ignores classification uncertainty: Treats class assignment perfect Attenuates effect sizes: Misclassification reduces observed differences Inflates Type error: Incorrect SE estimates

title: Analyzing Distal Outcomes with R3STEP
text: Key Differences: - R3STEP corrects classification error - Differences may subtle statistically important - Standard errors properly adjusted
code: # Compare naive vs R3STEP naive_means <- tapply(naive_data$delinquency, naive_data$class, mean) r3step_means <- result_bch@class_means$mean  comparison <- data.frame(   Class = 1:3,   Naive = naive_means,   R3STEP = r3step_means,   Difference = r3step_means - naive_means )  print(comparison) #   Class  Naive  R3STEP  Difference #   1      2.3    2.1      -0.2 #   2      4.1    4.3       0.2 #   3      6.8    7.2       0.4

title: Analyzing Distal Outcomes with R3STEP
text: surveymixr properly accounts survey design R3STEP analysis:
code: # R3STEP with full survey design result_survey <- r3step(   gmm_object = gmm_fit,  # Already includes strata, clusters, weights   distal_vars = "delinquency",   data = person_data,   method = "BCH" )  # Standard errors account for: # - Classification uncertainty # - Survey stratification # - Clustering (PSUs) # - Probability weights  # Compare to naive (ignoring survey design) result_naive <- r3step(   gmm_object = gmm_fit_no_survey,  # Fit without survey features   distal_vars = "delinquency",   data = person_data,   method = "BCH" )  # Survey-adjusted SEs will be larger (appropriately)

title: Analyzing Distal Outcomes with R3STEP
text: Distal Outcome Analysis examined whether three self-control trajectory classes differed adolescent delinquency using BCH method (Bolck et al. 2004) account classification uncertainty. overall test indicated significant differences across classes, χ2\chi^2(2) = 145.6, p < .001. Class 1 (high self-control; 55% sample) reported lowest delinquency (M = 2.1, SE = 0.15), followed Class 2 (moderate self-control; 30%; M = 4.3, SE = 0.18), Class 3 (low self-control; 15%; M = 7.2, SE = 0.22). pairwise comparisons statistically significant (ps < .001), effect sizes ranging medium large (Cohen’s d = 0.65 1.42).

code: # Compare BCH vs ML result_bch <- r3step(   gmm_object = gmm_fit,   distal_vars = "delinquency",   data = person_data,   method = "BCH" ) result_ml <- r3step(   gmm_object = gmm_fit,   distal_vars = "delinquency",   data = person_data,   method = "ML" )  # Extract means means_compare <- data.frame(   Class = 1:3,   BCH = result_bch@class_means$mean,   ML = result_ml@class_means$mean,   Difference = abs(result_bch@class_means$mean - result_ml@class_means$mean) )  print(means_compare)  # If differences are small (<0.1), results are robust

title: Analyzing Distal Outcomes with R3STEP
text: Q: Can include covariates Step 3? : Yes, manual 3-step approach allows custom models. However, covariates predicting class membership Step 1. Q: distal outcome count data? : Use appropriate family (Poisson/negative binomial) ML method transform BCH. Q: report paper? : Describe R3STEP procedure, cite Vermunt (2010), report omnibus test, class-specific means CIs, effect sizes. Q: Can use R3STEP growth factors (intercept/slope) distal? : typically - growth factors part model. Use multi-group GMM instead. Q: ordinal distal outcomes (e.g., Likert scales)? : Treat continuous ~5+ categories, use proportional odds model manual 3-step.

title: Real-World Analysis: Millennium Cohort Study Self-Control Trajectories
text: Research Question: children follow distinct developmental trajectories self-control early childhood late adolescence, trajectories associated later adolescent outcomes? Data Source: Millennium Cohort Study (MCS) - UK longitudinal birth cohort - Sample: Approximately 19,000 children born 2000-2002 - Design: Complex survey stratification clustering - Time Points: Ages 3, 5, 7, 11, 14, 17 years

title: Real-World Analysis: Millennium Cohort Study Self-Control Trajectories
text: Self-Control: Parent-reported measure child’s ability control impulses follow rules Delinquency: Self-reported antisocial behaviors age 17 Academic Achievement: Standardized test scores SES: Socioeconomic status (continuous measure) Survey Design: Nota Bene: simulated data based real MCS structure

text: Complex survey designs (stratification, clustering, weighting) common large-scale longitudinal studies often ignored statistical analysis. can lead : Incorrect standard errors (small large) Biased population estimates (unweighted) Invalid statistical tests (clustering ignored) surveymixr integrates survey design features seamlessly growth mixture modeling, ensuring statistically valid results.

text: : Weights adjust unequal selection probabilities non-response, making sample representative population. use: - ✅ Always, unless simple random sample - ✅ Large panel studies (MCS, Add Health, NLSY) - ✅ School-based surveys unequal selection - ✅ Strategies oversample minority populations Example: Millennium Cohort Study (MCS) oversampled: - Ethnic minority families - Low-income families - Families disadvantaged areas - Three four UK countries (Wales, Scotland, Northern Ireland) Without weights, results -represent groups reflect true UK population. specify: Key points: - Weights automatically normalized surveymixr - parameter estimates weighted M-step - Standard errors account weights using sandwich estimator

title: Survey Design Best Practices for Growth Mixture Modeling
text: : Dividing population homogeneous subgroups (strata) sampling independently . Impact: - Increases precision strata homogeneous - Ensures adequate sample size important subgroups - Standard errors may smaller stratification explains variance use: - ✅ Geographic stratification (countries, regions) - ✅ Socioeconomic stratification (income levels) - ✅ Institutional stratification (school types) Example: MCS stratified : - Country (England, Wales, Scotland, Northern Ireland) - Disadvantage status - Ethnic minority status (England) specify: Key points: - stratum ideally >= 2 PSUs - Standard errors typically decrease effective stratification
code: gmm_survey(   data = mcs_data,   strata = "stratum",  # Name of stratification variable   ... )

previous_headings: Survey Design in Growth Mixture Modeling: Best Practices > Survey Design Components
title: Survey Design Best Practices for Growth Mixture Modeling
text: : Sampling clusters (e.g., schools, neighborhoods) instead individuals, sampling within clusters. Impact: - Individuals within clusters correlated - Standard errors must account intra-cluster correlation - Ignoring clustering leads underestimated SEs (Type error inflation) use: - ✅ School-based sampling - ✅ Area-based sampling - ✅ Multi-stage sampling designs - ✅ individuals naturally cluster (families, classrooms) Example: MCS sampled electoral wards (clusters) first, families within wards. Children ward may similar children different wards due : - Shared neighborhood characteristics - Similar schools - Shared socioeconomic context specify: Key points: - Clusters must completely nested within strata - Must >= 2 clusters per stratum - Intra-cluster correlation typically increases SEs

text: Growth mixture models (GMMs) combine growth curve modeling latent class analysis identify distinct subgroups (classes) different developmental trajectories (Muthén Shedden 1999).

text: survey-weighted log-likelihood : ℓw(θ)=∑=1nwilog⁡f(yi|θ)\ell_w(\theta) = \sum_{=1}^n w_i \log f(y_i | \theta) wiw_i survey weight individual ii. Key innovation: surveymixr integrates survey weights directly EM algorithm, unlike post-hoc weighting approaches.

title: Technical Details and Algorithms
text: Combining GMM survey design: ℓw(θ)=∑=1nwilog⁡[∑k=1Kπk∏t=1Tif(yit|θk)]\ell_w(\theta) = \sum_{=1}^n w_i \log \left[ \sum_{k=1}^K \pi_k \prod_{t=1}^{T_i} f(y_{} | \theta_k) \right] : - wiw_i = survey weight - πk\pi_k = class proportion (weighted) - θk\theta_k = class-specific parameters - TiT_i = number observations individual ii

title: Technical Details and Algorithms
text: Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm (Dempster et al. 1977) iterates : E-step: Compute posterior class probabilities M-step: Update parameters given posterior probabilities

title: Technical Details and Algorithms
text: individual ii class kk: τik=wiπk∏t=1Tif(yit|θk)∑j=1Kwiπj∏t=1Tif(yit|θj)\tau_{ik} = \frac{w_i \pi_k \prod_{t=1}^{T_i} f(y_{} | \theta_k)}{\sum_{j=1}^K w_i \pi_j \prod_{t=1}^{T_i} f(y_{} | \theta_j)} τik=P(Ci=k|yi,θ)\tau_{ik} = P(C_i = k | y_i, \theta) posterior probability.

title: Technical Details and Algorithms
text: Class proportions (weighted): πk=∑=1nwiτik∑=1nwi\pi_k = \frac{\sum_{=1}^n w_i \tau_{ik}}{\sum_{=1}^n w_i} Growth parameters (class kk): Solve weighted regression: β̂k=arg⁡minβk∑=1n∑t=1Tiwiτik(yit−𝐗itTβk)2\hat{\beta}_k = \arg\min_{\beta_k} \sum_{=1}^n \sum_{t=1}^{T_i} w_i \tau_{ik} (y_{} - \mathbf{X}_{}^T \beta_k)^2 Variance (class kk): σ̂k2=∑=1n∑t=1Tiwiτik(yit−ŷ)2∑=1n∑t=1Tiwiτik\hat{\sigma}^2_k = \frac{\sum_{=1}^n \sum_{t=1}^{T_i} w_i \tau_{ik} (y_{} - \hat{y}_{})^2}{\sum_{=1}^n \sum_{t=1}^{T_i} w_i \tau_{ik}}

text: surveymixr uses Full Information Maximum Likelihood (FIML) missing data Missing Random (MAR) assumption. individual ii observed data yiobsy_i^{obs}: ℓw(θ|yiobs)=∑k=1Kwiτiklog⁡∏t∈obsif(yit|θk)\ell_w(\theta | y_i^{obs}) = \sum_{k=1}^K w_i \tau_{ik} \log \prod_{t \obs_i} f(y_{} | \theta_k) Advantages: - Uses available data - Unbiased MAR - need imputation

title: Technical Details and Algorithms
text: surveymixr uses sandwich (robust) variance estimator account : - Model misspecification - Clustering - Stratification 𝐕(θ̂)=𝐇−1𝐉𝐇−1\mathbf{V}(\hat{\theta}) = \mathbf{H}^{-1} \mathbf{J} \mathbf{H}^{-1} : - 𝐇\mathbf{H} = Hessian (observed information matrix) - 𝐉\mathbf{J} = Outer product score contributions (meat)

title: Technical Details and Algorithms
text: Clustering adjustment: 𝐉=∑h=1H∑c=1Ch(∑∈c𝐬i)(∑∈c𝐬i)T\mathbf{J} = \sum_{h=1}^H \sum_{c=1}^{C_h} \left(\sum_{\c} \mathbf{s}_i\right) \left(\sum_{\c} \mathbf{s}_i\right)^T : - HH = number strata - ChC_h = number clusters stratum hh - 𝐬i\mathbf{s}_i = score contribution individual ii Effect: Standard errors increase reflect within-cluster correlation (design effect > 1).

title: Technical Details and Algorithms
text: Since analytical derivatives complex, surveymixr uses numerical derivatives via numDeriv package: Hessian: Richardson extrapolation Gradient: Central differences Confidence intervals: θ̂±1.96×SE(θ̂)\hat{\theta} \pm 1.96 \times SE(\hat{\theta})

title: Technical Details and Algorithms
text: BLRT (McLachlan 1987) tests whether kk-class model fits better (k−1)(k-1)-class model.

title: Technical Details and Algorithms
text: Fit (k−1)(k-1)-class model, obtain θ̂k−1\hat{\theta}_{k-1} Fit kk-class model, obtain θ̂k\hat{\theta}_k Compute observed LRT statistic: LRTobs=2(ℓ(θ̂k)−ℓ(θ̂k−1))LRT_{obs} = 2(\ell(\hat{\theta}_k) - \ell(\hat{\theta}_{k-1})) Simulate data (k−1)(k-1)-class model Fit (k−1)(k-1) kk-class models Compute LRTbLRT_b pp-value = proportion LRTb>LRTobsLRT_b > LRT_{obs} Interpretation: - p<0.05p < 0.05: Reject (k−1)(k-1) classes, favor kk classes - p≥0.05p \geq 0.05: evidence kk classes Example:
code: selection <- gmm_select(   data = mcs_simulated,   id = "id",   time = "age",   outcome = "selfcontrol",   min_classes = 1,   max_classes = 5,   run_blrt = TRUE,   blrt_samples = 500,  # Bootstrap replicates   cores = 4 )  # View BLRT results summary(selection)

title: Technical Details and Algorithms
text: AIC (Akaike Information Criterion): AIC=−2ℓ(θ̂)+2pAIC = -2\ell(\hat{\theta}) + 2p BIC (Bayesian Information Criterion): BIC=−2ℓ(θ̂)+plog⁡(n)BIC = -2\ell(\hat{\theta}) + p \log(n) Sample-size adjusted BIC: aBIC=−2ℓ(θ̂)+plog⁡(n+224)aBIC = -2\ell(\hat{\theta}) + p \log\left(\frac{n+2}{24}\right) : - ℓ(θ̂)\ell(\hat{\theta}) = maximized log-likelihood - pp = number parameters - nn = sample size (effective sample size weighted data) Lower values indicate better fit.

title: Technical Details and Algorithms
text: Entropy measures classification certainty (Ramaswamy et al. 1993): E=1−∑=1n∑k=1Kτiklog⁡(τik)nlog⁡(K)E = 1 - \frac{\sum_{=1}^n \sum_{k=1}^K \tau_{ik} \log(\tau_{ik})}{n \log(K)} Range: [0,1][0, 1] Higher values = better classification E>0.8E > 0.8 considered good E>0.9E > 0.9 excellent

title: Technical Details and Algorithms
text: class kk: AvePPk=∑:arg⁡maxjτij=kτiknkAvePP_k = \frac{\sum_{: \arg\max_j \tau_{ij} = k} \tau_{ik}}{n_k} nkn_k = number individuals assigned class kk. Interpretation: - AvePP > 0.7 classes acceptable - AvePP > 0.8 good

title: Technical Details and Algorithms
text: OCCk=AvePPk/(1−AvePPk)πk/(1−πk)OCC_k = \frac{AvePP_k / (1 - AvePP_k)}{\pi_k / (1 - \pi_k)} πk\pi_k = class proportion. OCC > 5 indicates good classification

previous_headings: Part IV: Model Selection > Determining the Number of Classes
title: surveymixr User Manual
text: Lower better IC measures: Criteria: - BIC: Bayesian Information Criterion (commonly used) - aBIC: Sample-size adjusted BIC (large samples) - AIC: Akaike Information Criterion (less penalized) Decision Rule: - Choose model IC reaches minimum “elbow” - Lower values indicate better fit - Balance fit vs. parsimony
code: # Compare models with different class counts selection <- gmm_select(   data = mcs_simulated,   id = "id",   time = "age",   outcome = "selfcontrol",   classes = 1:5,              # Test 1-5 classes   strata = "stratum",   cluster = "psu",   weights = "weight",   criteria = c("BIC", "aBIC", "entropy"),   starts = 200,   cores = 4 )  # View results print(selection) plot_model_selection(selection)

text: Gold standard class enumeration: Interpretation: - Tests k-class vs. (k-1)-class model - Significant p-value → k-class model better - Stop p-value becomes non-significant

title: surveymixr User Manual
text: Problem: Direct inclusion auxiliary variables (e.g., demographics, outcomes) GMM can: - Alter class formation - Lead biased estimates - Change class membership Solution: R3STEP performs auxiliary analysis class formation, accounting classification uncertainty.

previous_headings: Part VII: Auxiliary Variable Analysis > The R3STEP Approach
title: surveymixr User Manual
text: Use R3STEP : - Compare classes distal outcomes (e.g., academic achievement) - Examine demographic differences classes - Test predictors class membership - Avoid bias classification error

previous_headings: Part VII: Auxiliary Variable Analysis > The R3STEP Approach
title: surveymixr User Manual
code: # Step 1: Fit GMM (without auxiliary variables) fit <- gmm_survey(   data = mcs_simulated,   id = "id", time = "age", outcome = "selfcontrol",   n_classes = 3,   strata = "stratum", cluster = "psu", weights = "weight",   starts = 500 )  # Step 2: Prepare distal variables (one row per individual) distal_data <- mcs_simulated[!duplicated(mcs_simulated$id), ]  # Step 3: R3STEP analysis r3step_results <- r3step(   gmm_object = fit,   distal_vars = c("academic_achievement", "delinquency", "ses"),   data = distal_data,   method = "BCH"             # or "ML", "manual" )

text: Interpretation: - Omnibus test: overall differences? - Pairwise tests: classes differ? - Effect sizes: large differences? (d > 0.5 = medium, d > 0.8 = large)
code: # Comprehensive summary summary(r3step_results)  # Class-specific means for distal variables print(r3step_results@class_means)  # Omnibus tests (overall differences across classes) print(r3step_results@test_results)  # Effect sizes (Cohen's d for pairwise comparisons) print(r3step_results@effect_sizes)

title: surveymixr User Manual
text: Red Flags: - ⚠️ Best solution replicated <10% time - ⚠️ Multiple distinct local maxima - ⚠️ Wide range log-likelihood values Solutions: - Increase starts (e.g., 500 → 1000) - Try different initialization methods - Consider simpler model (fewer classes)

text: surveymixr uses Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm: E-Step: Compute posterior probabilities P(Ci=k|Yi)=πkf(Yi|θk)∑j=1Kπjf(Yi|θj)P(C_i = k | Y_i) = \frac{\pi_k f(Y_i | \theta_k)}{\sum_{j=1}^K \pi_j f(Y_i | \theta_j)} M-Step: Update parameters θ(t+1)=arg⁡maxθ∑=1N∑k=1KP(Ci=k|Yi;θ(t))log⁡f(Yi|θk)\theta^{(t+1)} = \arg\max_\theta \sum_{=1}^N \sum_{k=1}^K P(C_i=k|Y_i;\theta^{(t)}) \log f(Y_i|\theta_k)

title: surveymixr User Manual
text: Sandwich estimator: Var(θ̂)=H−1ΣH−1\text{Var}(\hat{\theta}) = H^{-1} \Sigma H^{-1} : - HH = Hessian matrix - Σ\Sigma = Survey-adjusted score covariance

title: Growth Mixture Models with Complex Survey Design
text: surveymixr implements growth mixture modeling (GMM) longitudinal data full integration complex survey design features including stratification, clustering, probability weights. package fills critical gap R’s statistical capabilities enabling analyses large-scale longitudinal surveys (e.g., Millennium Cohort Study, Add Health, NLSY) previously possible proprietary software like Mplus. Read complete User Manual comprehensive documentation covering features, workflows, best practices.

title: Growth Mixture Models with Complex Survey Design
text: Survey Design Integration: Proper handling stratification, clustering (PSUs), probability weights sandwich standard errors Bootstrap Likelihood Ratio Test (BLRT): Efficient parallelized implementation optimal class enumeration Multiple Random Starts: Convergence diagnostics tracking local maxima (500-1000+ starts) R3STEP Method: Auxiliary variable analysis classification uncertainty correction (BCH, ML, manual approaches) Flexible Growth Models: Linear, quadratic, nonlinear, free basis time scores Comprehensive Diagnostics: Entropy, class proportions, classification quality, convergence tracking Professional Visualization: Publication-ready trajectory plots confidence intervals Multiple Outcome Types: Continuous, count, binary, ordinal outcomes

title: Detect Influential Observations in GMM — diagnose_influence
text: **Note:** function requires original data stored fitted object. Make sure fit model keep_data = TRUE. **Cook's Distance (Survey-Weighted):** Measures influence observation parameter estimates simultaneously. survey-weighted version accounts sampling weights: $$D_i = \frac{(\hat{\beta} - \hat{\beta}_{(-)})' X'WX (\hat{\beta} - \hat{\beta}_{(-)})}{p \hat{\sigma}^2}$$ W diagonal weight matrix. **DFBETAS:** Measures influence observation individual parameters: $$DFBETAS_{ij} = \frac{\hat{\beta}_j - \hat{\beta}_{j(-)}}{SE(\hat{\beta}_{j(-)})}$$ **Leverage:** Identifies observations unusual predictor patterns: $$h_i = X_i (X'WX)^{-1} X_i' w_i$$

title: Detect Influential Observations in GMM — diagnose_influence
text: Cook, R. D. (1977). Detection influential observation linear regression. *Technometrics*, 19(1), 15-18. Pfeffermann, D., & Sverchkov, M. (1999). Parametric semi-parametric estimation regression models fitted survey data. *Sankhyā: Indian Journal Statistics, Series B*, 61(1), 166-186.

title: Entropy Function (Exported) — entropy
text: Numeric entropy value 0 1, values closer 1   indicate better class separation

title: Entropy Function (Exported) — entropy
text: Entropy measures certainty classification mixture models. calculated : $$E = 1 - \frac{\sum_i \sum_k p_{ik} \log(p_{ik})}{N \log(K)}$$ \(p_{ik}\) posterior probability individual belonging class k, N sample size, K number classes. Values range 0 (complete uncertainty, uniform classification) 1 (perfect classification). Values 0.80 generally indicate good class separation.

title: Entropy Function (Exported) — entropy
text: Ramaswamy, V., DeSarbo, W. S., Reibstein, D. J., & Robinson, W. T. (1993). empirical pooling approach estimating marketing mix elasticities PIMS data. Marketing Science, 12(1), 103-124.

title: K-Fold Cross-Validation for GMM Model Selection — gmm_cv
text: Cross-validation mixture models requires special considerations: **1. Survey Design Preservation:** stratified_cv = TRUE, folds maintain proportion observations stratum, preserving survey design structure. **2. Individual-Level Splitting:** data split individual level (observation level) keep time points person together. **3. Prediction Metrics:** Multiple metrics computed: - Log-likelihood held-data - Classification accuracy (true classes known) - Mean squared prediction error - Weighted metrics using survey weights **4. Label Switching:** Class labels may differ across folds. algorithm attempts align labels based trajectory patterns.

title: Model Selection for Growth Mixture Models — gmm_select
text: function systematically compares mixture models different numbers latent classes. Multiple criteria available: Information Criteria: BIC: Bayesian Information Criterion (lower better) AIC: Akaike Information Criterion (lower better) aBIC: Sample-size adjusted BIC (lower better) Classification Quality: Entropy: Classification certainty (higher better, >0.8 preferred) Hypothesis Testing: BLRT: Bootstrap Likelihood Ratio Test comparing K vs K-1 classes.     Considered gold standard class enumeration. significant p-value     (< 0.05) indicates K classes fit better K-1 classes. BLRT implementation uses parametric bootstrap: data generated K-1 class model, distribution likelihood ratio statistics computed empirically. computationally intensive provides reliable test class enumeration. Practical Considerations: Increase starts (500-1000) final model selection BLRT computationally intensive; use fewer bootstrap samples     initial exploration Smallest class typically >5 Consider substantive interpretability alongside statistical criteria

title: Growth Mixture Model for Count Outcomes — gmm_survey_count
text: count outcomes, model uses: $$Y_{} | C_i = k \sim Poisson(\lambda_{itk})$$ \(\log(\lambda_{itk}) = \eta_{itk}\) \(\eta_{itk}\) includes growth parameters. zero-inflated models: $$P(Y_{} = 0 | C_i = k) = \pi_k + (1 - \pi_k) \times e^{-\lambda_{itk}}$$ $$P(Y_{} = y | C_i = k) = (1 - \pi_k) \times Poisson(y; \lambda_{itk}), \quad y > 0$$

title: Growth Mixture Model with Time-Varying Covariates — gmm_survey_tvc
text: **Model Specifications:** **1. Direct Effects Model:** $$Y_{} = \beta_{0k} + \beta_{1k} t + \gamma_k X_{} + \epsilon_{}$$ \(X_{}\) time-varying covariate \(\gamma_k\) class-specific effect outcome. **2. Indirect Effects Model:** $$Y_{} = \beta_{0k} + (\beta_{1k} + \delta_k \bar{X}_i) t + \epsilon_{}$$ \(\bar{X}_i\) individual mean TVC \(\delta_k\) represents TVC affects growth rate. **3. Effects Model:** $$Y_{} = \beta_{0k} + (\beta_{1k} + \delta_k \bar{X}_i) t + \gamma_k (X_{} - \bar{X}_i) + \epsilon_{}$$ separates -person effects (\(\delta_k\)) within-person effects (\(\gamma_k\)). **4. Interaction Model:** $$Y_{} = \beta_{0k} + \beta_{1k} t + \gamma_k X_{} + \lambda_k (t \times X_{}) + \epsilon_{}$$ \(\lambda_k\) captures TVC moderates trajectory slope. **Time-Varying vs Time-Invariant:** - **Time-invariant**: Constant individual (e.g., sex, baseline SES) - **Time-varying**: Changes within individuals (e.g., parental monitoring, stress) function automatically detects covariates time-varying checking within-individual variance. **Centering:** center_tvc = TRUE, covariates centered grand mean. improves interpretability can aid convergence. "" effects, person-mean centering used separate within- -person effects. **Lagged Effects:** Set tvc_lag > 0 examine lagged effects TVCs: - tvc_lag = 1: Previous time point predicts current outcome - tvc_lag = 2: Two time points back predicts current outcome

title: Lo-Mendell-Rubin Test for Class Enumeration — lmr_test
text: LMR test (Lo, Mendell, & Rubin, 2001) tests null hypothesis k-1 classes sufficient alternative k classes. test statistic : $$LRT = -2(\log L_{k-1} - \log L_k)$$ regularity conditions, follows asymptotic distribution can approximated. adjusted LMR (aLMR) applies scaling correction better finite-sample performance: $$aLMR = LMR \times c$$ c scaling factor based sample size model complexity. **Advantages BLRT:** - Much faster (bootstrap resampling) - Asymptotic approximation - Good performance large samples **Disadvantages:** - Less accurate BLRT small samples - Relies asymptotic theory - May anti-conservative

title: Lo-Mendell-Rubin Test for Class Enumeration — lmr_test
text: Lo, Y., Mendell, N. R., & Rubin, D. B. (2001). Testing number components normal mixture. *Biometrika*, 88(3), 767-778. Nylund, K. L., Asparouhov, T., & Muthén, B. O. (2007). Deciding number classes latent class analysis growth mixture modeling: Monte Carlo simulation study. *Structural Equation Modeling*, 14(4), 535-569.

title: R3STEP Analysis of Auxiliary Variables — r3step
text: R3STEP approach addresses key challenge mixture modeling: naively relating class membership auxiliary variables using -likely class assignment leads biased estimates due classification uncertainty. R3STEP? Traditional approaches use -likely class assignment ("classify-analyze") produce biased parameter estimates incorrect standard errors. R3STEP methods correct incorporating classification uncertainty analysis. Available Methods: BCH (default): Uses weighted regression weights derived     classification error matrix. Computationally efficient     recommended applications. ML: Simultaneous estimation mixture model auxiliary     variable relationships. accurate computationally intensive. Manual 3-step: Traditional 3-step approach manual     correction classification error. function automatically accounts complex survey design features (weights, clustering, stratification) computing standard errors test statistics. Interpretation: output provides: Class-specific means (adjusted classification error) Survey-adjusted standard errors Omnibus tests (overall class differences) Pairwise comparisons (requested) Effect sizes (Cohen's d survey weights)

text: function generates data following growth mixture model: individual class k: $$y_{} = (\beta_{0k} + u_{0i}) + (\beta_{1k} + u_{1i}) * t + \epsilon_{}$$ : \(\beta_{0k}\), \(\beta_{1k}\) class-specific intercept slope \(u_{0i}\), \(u_{1i}\) random effects (optional, yet implemented) \(\epsilon_{}\) ~ N(0, \(\sigma_k^2\)) residuals Survey design features: Stratification: Population divided strata, sampling within strata Clustering: Individuals nested within PSUs (e.g., schools, neighborhoods) Weights: Inverse probability weights account unequal selection probabilities function can generate various missing data patterns test robustness analyses.
